title: UGC for food brands Australia: formats and hooks | MANA
description: UGC for food brands in Australia: the formats and hooks that work, a checklist for the first batch, and how a monthly creator video program runs.
h1: UGC for food brands in Australia: formats, hooks and how a monthly program runs
lede: UGC for food and beverage brands in Australia works best as short, first-person video shot at the moment of use: the fridge opening, the lid coming off, the first sip, the post-gym shake. The pattern that holds up is a paid pilot of a small batch across two or three formats, then a monthly program that keeps the format that won and replaces the hooks every few weeks.

sections.h2: What does UGC for food brands in Australia look like?
body: Food and drink has an advantage most categories do not: the product is consumed on camera. The formats that work put the product in a real moment of use and keep the camera close enough to see texture.

Six formats carry most of it. The first bite or first sip, filmed in one take with real sound. The fridge or pantry restock, where the product lands next to things the viewer already buys. The routine placement: morning coffee, post-gym, school lunch, night shift. The three-ways recipe, cut fast, which needs no script. The delivery or unboxing, which suits subscription, frozen and meal kits. And the label read, where the creator turns the pack over and talks through what is in it.
Shoot vertical, in a real kitchen or café, lit by a window. Studio food styling reads as an advertisement inside the first second, and the first second is the one you cannot afford to lose.

sections.h2: Which hooks work for food and drink?
body: A hook is the first three seconds plus the first line on screen. Four kinds hold up in this category: the objection ("I assumed this would taste like cardboard"), the swap ("this replaced my 3pm coffee"), the specific habit ("I have had this every morning for three weeks"), and the visual tease, where the pour or the pull-apart happens before anyone speaks.
Write five hooks per concept and film all five against the same body footage. One video then becomes five tests, and you learn which claim earns attention before you spend more on production.

Health, nutrition and ingredient claims carry rules, so the brief has to say what a creator may and may not say. That is a writing job, not a call: [how to brief a creator](/journal/how-to-brief-a-creator) covers what to put down before anything is filmed.

sections.h2: What should a food brand lock before the first batch?
body: Use this as the checklist for a pilot. Everything on it is cheaper to decide now than to fix in revisions.
bullets: The one thing every video must show on screen, such as product in hand with the label legible
Two or three formats to test, not six
Five hook lines per concept, filmed against the same body footage
What a creator may and may not claim about health, nutrition or ingredients
Allergen, storage and preparation notes, so nothing is filmed wrong
Usage term, platforms, and whether you will whitelist from the creator's handle
Delivery specs: vertical, raw plus edited, burnt-in captions off, a clean audio track
Who approves, and the date they approve by

sections.h2: How does a monthly program run?
body: MANA runs food and beverage work as a paid pilot first, then a monthly program. The pilot is a small batch across the two or three formats above: we cast from the roster, write the briefs, get product to the creators, run one revision round, check every cut, and hand back ad-ready files plus raw footage. Casting comes from a managed roster of [UGC creators in Australia](/ugc-creators-australia) rather than an open marketplace, which is why the same brief does not have to be re-explained each month.

From the second month on, the cycle repeats on a fixed date. The winning format stays, its hooks get replaced, the tired cuts get retired, and the videos can run as Spark Ads or Partnership Ads from the creators' handles inside your own ad account. For brands outside Australia, the same programs run at [MANA Creators](https://manacreators.com/).

A common way it goes wrong: a brand books ten creators for ten different concepts, receives ten one-off videos, and has nothing it can repeat next month. A second common failure is a 30-day usage window, which forces you to pull the one ad that was working. Both are decided before filming, which is why [usage rights and whitelisting](/journal/usage-rights-and-whitelisting-explained-for-brands) belongs in the pilot scope and not in a later email.

sections.h2: How do you judge whether a food video worked?
body: Three numbers, in order. Hook rate: three-second views over impressions, which tells you if the first line earned attention. Hold rate: how many viewers reach the point where the product is shown. Then cost per add-to-cart or CPA, once there is enough spend behind it to mean anything.

Saves and shares matter more in food than in most categories, because people keep recipes and send drinks to a friend. Here is the shape of that on our own roster: Kevin Chiang's Instagram insights for a 30-day window in June 2026 show 928K+ views, 40K average reel views, 92% non-follower reach, 109K interactions, 34.7K saves and 12.3K shares. Roughly a third of that response was people keeping the video to act on later, not just reacting to it. Preston Young's 90-day insights for June to September 2026 show 1.86M views and 86.6% non-follower reach, which is the argument for pairing organic reach with paid: the video travels well past the follower count.
A worked example from ordinary monthly work: in September 2026 a creator on the roster delivered UGC for a nutrition brand, brief to final cut, under the same process described above.

faq: How many videos does a food brand need each month?

Enough to replace creative as it fatigues in your ad account, which depends on spend and how many formats you run. Start with a pilot batch across two or three formats, find the one with the best hook rate, then commit to a fixed monthly number built around it.
Do the creators have to be food creators?

No. Audience fit and the ability to film a believable moment of use matter more than a food-only feed. A creator on our roster delivered UGC for a nutrition brand in September 2026, and their main lane is architecture and design.
Who owns the videos, and can we run them as ads?

Whatever the agreement says, which is why the usage term, the platforms, the whitelisting permission and any category exclusivity are written down before filming. Ad-ready files plus raw footage are delivered, and the cuts can run as Spark Ads or Partnership Ads from the creator's handle in your account.
